title: Title, date and occasion
short: Wordsworth revisits the Wye valley on 13 July 1798, five years after a solitary walking tour there in August 1793.
body: The full 1798 title reads 'Lines written a few miles above Tintern Abbey, on revisiting the banks of the Wye during a tour, July 13, 1798'. Wordsworth later recalled beginning it on leaving Tintern and finishing it as he entered Bristol after a four- or five-day ramble with his sister, adding that not a line was altered or written down until he reached Bristol (Fenwick note). The 1793 visit came when he was a lonely, politically troubled young man after his time in revolutionary France. The poem was placed last in Lyrical Ballads (1798), where it stands apart from the ballads in its meditative blank verse. Marjorie Levinson noted that the date falls on the eve of Bastille Day and argued that the poem's careful framing keeps history, poverty and industry out of view; other critics, such as Hartman, read it chiefly as a drama of memory and consciousness. The insistent counting ('five... five... five') stresses how much time, and inner change, lies between the two visits.

title: inland murmur
short: Wordsworth's own note explains that the Wye a few miles above Tintern is not affected by the tides.
body: Wordsworth glossed this phrase in 1798: the river is 'not affected by the tides a few miles above Tintern'. Lower down, near Chepstow, the Wye is a muddy tidal river; upstream it is a fresh, flowing stream heard rather than seen. The word 'inland' therefore places the speaker exactly and also suggests something interior and sheltered, a sound set apart from the sea and the outside world. 'Murmur' is the first of the poem's many soft sound-words (compare 'the still, sad music of humanity'). Hearing comes before seeing in the opening: 'again I hear' precedes 'Do I behold', so the landscape enters first through the ear.

title: hedge-rows, hardly hedge-rows
short: The speaker corrects himself: the hedges have grown so wild they barely count as hedges; cultivated land is fading back into nature.
body: The self-correction makes us watch the mind looking and revising, a typical Wordsworthian move. The lines describe a landscape on the border of farm and wilderness: cottage plots and orchards that 'lose themselves' among the woods, and farms 'green to the very door'. The Wye was famous in the 1780s and 1790s as a picturesque tour, popularised by William Gilpin's Observations on the River Wye (1782), and the lines show Wordsworth's familiarity with that way of seeing, while preferring calm harmony ('Nor... disturb / The wild green landscape') to the picturesque taste for rough contrasts.

title: vagrant dwellers... hermit
short: Smoke rising among the trees is guessed to come from homeless wanderers or a hermit; critics debate what the guess leaves out.
body: The 'wreathes of smoke' give only 'uncertain notice' of who is there; the speaker imagines either 'vagrant dwellers in the houseless woods' (vagrants, wanderers without houses) or a solitary hermit. The hermit turns the scene into a contemplative image of the poet himself. Historicist critics, above all Marjorie Levinson, have pointed out that the real Wye valley in the 1790s held charcoal-burners, iron works and many poor people (Gilpin had noticed beggars living about the Abbey ruins) and argued that the poem converts social fact into peaceful landscape. Others reply that the vagrants are in fact acknowledged here, and that the poem's subject is the mind rather than the economy. 'Houseless' is a strong word, recalling King Lear's 'houseless heads' on the heath.

title: a landscape to a blind man's eye
short: In absence the remembered landscape has not been lost to him, as a scene is lost on a blind man.
body: The negative simile states the key claim of the second paragraph: memory has kept 'these forms of beauty' alive. 'Forms' is a weighty word for Wordsworth, meaning the shapes and outlines of nature that impress themselves on the mind (compare 'Their colours and their forms' later and 'a mansion for all lovely forms' at the end). The lines also introduce the poem's arc of eye imagery, which runs through 'an eye made quiet', 'the mighty world / Of eye and ear', and Dorothy's 'wild eyes'.

title: sensations sweet, felt in the blood
short: Memories of nature act first as bodily sensation, then pass into the 'purer mind', a sequence drawn from eighteenth-century associationist psychology.
body: The lines trace a progression from body to mind: sensations are 'felt in the blood, and felt along the heart' and then pass 'even into my purer mind / With tranquil restoration'. Editors relate this to David Hartley's associationist psychology (Observations on Man, 1749), which Coleridge admired in the 1790s and which explained how simple sensations combine into complex ideas and moral feelings. The phrase 'tranquil restoration' looks forward to Wordsworth's 1800 definition of poetry's origin in 'emotion recollected in tranquillity'. The repetition 'felt... felt' imitates the slow pulse it describes.

title: little, nameless, unremembered acts
short: The forgotten pleasures of nature may have shaped small kindnesses that are themselves forgotten: nature's moral influence works unseen.
body: The claim is carefully hedged ('such, perhaps, / As may have had no trivial influence'), typical of the poem's tentative tone. Unremembered pleasures produce unremembered acts of kindness, so the moral effect of nature lies below conscious memory. The idea that small habitual feelings form character belongs to Wordsworth's programme in Lyrical Ballads and to associationist thinking. The triple adjective slows the line and enacts the modesty it praises. Critics often contrast this quiet 'best portion of a good man's life' with the heroic ethics of earlier poetry.

title: burthen of the mystery
short: 'Burthen' is an older spelling of 'burden'; the 'mystery' is the baffling weight of an 'unintelligible world'.
body: 'Burthen' (Old English byrthen, from beran, to bear) is the load the 'blessed mood' lightens; the word can also mean a refrain in a song, and some readers hear that second sense too. 'Mystery' carries religious weight (Greek mysterion, a secret rite or revealed truth), but here it is the oppressive puzzle of existence, the 'heavy and the weary weight / Of all this unintelligible world'. The repeated 'In which... In which' builds the passage like a liturgical period. The phrase became famous enough for Keats to adopt it in his letter on the 'Mansion of Many Apartments' (3 May 1818), where he says Wordsworth was exploring the 'burden of the Mystery'.

title: a living soul
short: In the 'blessed mood' the body seems suspended and the speaker becomes, in Genesis's words, 'a living soul'.
body: The phrase echoes Genesis 2:7, where God breathes into Adam's nostrils 'the breath of life; and man became a living soul'; Paul repeats it in 1 Corinthians 15:45. Wordsworth reverses the biblical order in a striking way: here it is the suspension of breath ('the breath of this corporeal frame... / Almost suspended') that brings about the new life of the soul. The passage describes a trance-like state close to mystical experience, though the poem avoids explicit Christian doctrine. 'Corporeal frame' (bodily structure) is eighteenth-century diction.

title: the life of things
short: A quietened eye, made calm by 'harmony' and 'joy', sees past surfaces into the living principle of the world.
body: The climax of the second paragraph. Sight here is no longer the eager, physical seeing of youth (the youthful passion for 'colours and their forms', which he calls 'an appetite') but 'an eye made quiet', an inward vision. 'Harmony' and 'joy' are 'powers', not just feelings. 'The life of things' implies that nature is alive throughout, an idea that prepares for the 'motion and a spirit' later. Readers differ on whether this is mystical (Bradley), philosophical (influenced by Coleridge's interest in unitarian and pantheist ideas in 1798), or a psychological account of deep calm. Note that the very next line ('If this / Be but a vain belief') immediately raises a doubt.

title: If this be but a vain belief
short: The speaker immediately concedes that his vision may be illusion, yet insists on its consoling power anyway.
body: This is one of the poem's characteristic hedges (compare 'I trust', 'I would believe', 'Nor, perchance'). Critics read the hesitations in different ways: as honest scepticism about mystical claims, as the rhythm of a mind thinking aloud, or (with Levinson and others) as a sign that the poem's affirmations are under strain. The paragraph then turns to the opposite of the blessed mood: the 'fretful stir / Unprofitable, and the fever of the world', city life and anxiety, against which the Wye remains a refuge. 'Unprofitable' recalls Hamlet's 'weary, stale, flat, and unprofitable' world (Hamlet 1.2).

title: apostrophe to the Wye
short: The speaker turns to address the river directly, a raised, ode-like gesture.
body: Apostrophe (direct address to an absent or inanimate thing) marks the emotional peak of the paragraph; 'sylvan' (Latin silva, a wood) means wooded. Wordsworth told readers in a note added in 1800 that he had not ventured to call the poem an ode but hoped its transitions and 'impassioned music' would recall that form. The paragraph structure, with turns and returns, does resemble the 'greater Romantic lyric' that M. H. Abrams described: a speaker in a specific landscape, a meditation that moves away and returns with new understanding. The river as 'wanderer' mirrors the speaker's own wanderings.

title: like a roe
short: The young Wordsworth bounded over the hills like a deer, a simile with biblical roots.
body: A roe is a small deer. The Song of Solomon repeatedly compares the lover to 'a roe or a young hart' upon the mountains (2:9, 2:17, 8:14), and the echo gives his youthful energy a Hebraic, lyrical colour. The speaker then complicates the picture: in 1793 he was 'more like a man / Flying from something that he dreads, than one / Who sought the thing he loved'. Biographers connect this flight with his guilt and distress after leaving Annette Vallon and their daughter in France and with his disillusionment over the Revolution and Britain's war with France, though the poem itself names nothing.

title: the sounding cataract / haunted me like a passion
short: In youth nature was an 'appetite', felt with the intensity of passion and needing no thought to give it meaning.
body: A cataract is a waterfall. The verb 'Haunted' and the simile 'like a passion' make the youthful love of nature obsessive, almost erotic. These were feelings with 'no need of a remoter charm, / By thought supplied', that is, they did not require associations or ideas to make them attractive. This marks the second of the three stages critics often find in the poem's account of growth: the 'glad animal movements' of boyhood, the passionate 'appetite' of youth, and the mature, thoughtful love of nature that follows. The later Prelude develops the same scheme at length.

title: aching joys... dizzy raptures
short: Oxymoronic phrases sum up the intense, almost painful pleasures of youth, now gone.
body: 'Aching joys' joins pleasure and pain; 'dizzy raptures' suggests ecstasy that unbalances the mind ('rapture', from Latin rapere, to seize, means being carried away). Their loss leads into a crucial statement: 'Not for this / Faint I, nor mourn nor murmur'. The inversion and alliteration ('mourn nor murmur') give the line a formal, almost biblical firmness. The theme of loss compensated by 'other gifts' is the basis of what critics call Wordsworth's poetry of compensation, later restated in the 'Intimations' Ode ('We will grieve not, rather find / Strength in what remains behind').

title: recompence
short: Compensation: the mature mind gains thought and moral feeling in return for lost youthful intensity.
body: 'Recompence' is an old spelling of 'recompense', repayment or compensation. The phrase is hedged ('I would believe'), so the poem offers its consolation as a belief rather than a certainty. Critics such as Hartman have stressed how much of Wordsworth's major poetry depends on this exchange of immediate experience for reflective consciousness, and how anxious the exchange can be. The language of profit and loss here (gifts, recompence, 'owed') runs through the poem and contrasts with the 'unprofitable' fever of the world.

anchor: The still, sad music of humanity
title: the still, sad music of humanity
short: The mature man hears human suffering within nature, a quiet music that chastens rather than jars.
body: This is the first gain of maturity: nature is no longer seen in isolation but with an awareness of human life and sorrow. 'Still' means quiet and also continuing; 'sad' adds solemnity. The music is 'Not harsh nor grating, though of ample power / To chasten and subdue', so it disciplines the self without disturbing it. Critics of the poem's politics ask whether this abstract 'humanity' stands in for the real poverty of the Wye valley, while others see in it the ethical heart of Lyrical Ballads, a collection about the rural poor. The paradox of a 'still' music (silent yet heard) suggests a sound perceived by the mind rather than the ear.

title: something far more deeply interfused
short: A 'presence', 'a motion and a spirit', dwells in all of nature and in the mind; readers dispute whether this is pantheism.
body: 'Interfused' means poured through and mingled with. The passage describes one spirit present in light, ocean, air, sky 'and in the mind of man', which 'impels / All thinking things, all objects of all thought, / And rolls through all things'. It dissolves the line between thinking subject and object thought about. Its closest contemporary parallels are in Coleridge's 1790s poems ('The Eolian Harp', 'Religious Musings'), and editors also mention Spinoza, Newtonian ideas of a pervasive ether, and Virgil's 'spiritus intus alit' (Aeneid 6.726). Early readers, and later Wordsworth himself in revising other poems, worried that such passages were pantheistic rather than Christian; others call the view panentheist or simply Romantic natural piety.

title: what they half-create, and what perceive
short: Perception is partly creative: the senses half make the world they see. Wordsworth's own note points to Edward Young.
body: Wordsworth's 1798 note says the line closely resembles an admirable line of Young whose exact words he could not recall: Edward Young's Night Thoughts (Night 6) speaks of the senses that 'half create the wondrous world they see'. The idea is central to Romantic theories of imagination: the mind is not a passive mirror but an active partner with nature (compare Coleridge's account of the 'primary imagination' in Biographia Literaria, ch. 13). The phrase 'the language of the sense' makes nature a language read through the senses. The following lines pile up titles for nature (anchor, nurse, guide, guardian, soul), a list critics have called both moving and strained.

title: genial spirits
short: 'Genial' here means of one's native creative powers; the phrase echoes Milton's Samson.
body: In Samson Agonistes Samson laments, 'So much I feel my genial spirits droop' (l. 594). 'Genial' (Latin genialis, from genius, the inborn spirit, also connected with generation) means relating to one's vital, creative nature, not merely 'cheerful'. The fear of their decay was a shared worry in the circle: Coleridge would echo the same phrase in 'Dejection: An Ode' (1802), 'My genial spirits fail'. Here the speaker says that even if he lacked his philosophy of nature, he would not let his spirits fail, because Dorothy is with him.

title: my dearest Friend... my dear, dear Sister
short: The poem's listener, revealed only now, is Dorothy Wordsworth, in whom the poet sees his own former self.
body: Dorothy Wordsworth (1771-1855), the poet's sister and companion, kept the journals that underlie several of his poems. Her late appearance transforms the poem into a conversation poem like Coleridge's 'Frost at Midnight', addressed to a silent listener. He reads 'my former pleasures in the shooting lights / Of thy wild eyes', so she embodies the earlier stage of his own development. Feminist critics, notably Margaret Homans, have objected that Dorothy is denied a mature mind of her own and serves as a mirror for her brother's growth; others stress the poem's tenderness and its prayer for her future. The repeated 'dear, dear' is unusually intimate for the period's blank verse.

title: Nature never did betray the heart that loved her
short: A confident statement of faith in nature's goodness, framed as a prayer for Dorothy.
body: The poem's most absolute claim, made in the language of prayer ('this prayer I make'). Nature is personified as a faithful female guide who leads 'from joy to joy'. Some readers find the assertion bold beyond what the poem has earned, given the earlier doubts ('If this / Be but a vain belief'); others take it as a deliberate act of faith. The following list of social evils ('evil tongues, / Rash judgments... the sneers of selfish men') reflects the hostility Wordsworth and Coleridge felt as suspected radicals in 1797-98, when they were watched by a government agent at Alfoxden.

title: evil tongues
short: Echoes Milton, who describes himself fallen 'on evil days... and evil tongues'.
body: At the start of Paradise Lost Book 7, Milton, blind and politically defeated after the Restoration, speaks of himself as 'fall'n on evil days, / On evil days though fall'n, and evil tongues' (7.25-26). Wordsworth borrows the phrase to align his own position as a misjudged, isolated poet with Milton's. 'Greetings where no kindness is' and 'the dreary intercourse of daily life' (intercourse meaning social dealings) widen the list to the hollowness of ordinary society. Milton is a constant presence in Wordsworth's blank verse.

anchor: a mansion for all lovely forms
title: a mansion... a dwelling-place
short: Dorothy's mature mind and memory will become a house storing beautiful forms and sounds, as the poet's own has done.
body: The architectural metaphor (mansion, from Latin manere, to stay, 'dwelling-place') turns memory into a home in which experience is kept. It closes the circle of the poem: the poet has been describing how his own memory sustained him during five years of absence; now he projects the same process onto Dorothy, whose 'wild ecstasies' will mature 'into a sober pleasure'. The final lines imagine his own absence or death ('where I no more can hear / Thy voice'), so the poem ends by asking to be remembered within that mansion of memory. Keats's well-known 'Mansion of Many Apartments' letter (3 May 1818) uses a different mansion, the house of life, but it is in that letter that he quotes this poem's 'burden of the Mystery'.

title: blank verse and the closing return
short: Unrhymed iambic pentameter in verse paragraphs; the last lines return to the opening landscape, closing the circle.
body: The poem is written in blank verse, the metre of Milton's Paradise Lost and of Cowper's The Task, arranged in five verse paragraphs of unequal length. Heavy enjambment and long periodic sentences give it the movement of thought rather than song. The ending deliberately repeats the opening ('these steep woods and lofty cliffs', 'many years / Of absence'), but now the landscape is 'More dear, both for themselves, and for thy sake': loved for its own sake and through Dorothy. Critics call this circular structure, returning to the starting point with deepened understanding, the hallmark of the 'greater Romantic lyric'.
